Parties approaching the Supreme Court under Article 136 have a duty to disclose all material facts, including the existence of stay orders affecting the subject matter. Non-disclosure vitiates the proceedings.

The declaration under this section on September 20, 1977, triggered the timeline for the award under Section 11-A. The date of this declaration is crucial for determining whether the statutory period for making the award had expired.

rules.reference: Effect of stay orders on limitation periods
rules.relevance: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act excludes periods where proceedings are stayed by a court order from the two-year limitation period. The existence of the interim stay orders obtained by the petitioners is relevant to determining if the award was actually time-barred.

These rules govern the procedure for filing Special Leave Petitions, including the requirement to file an affidavit disclosing material facts. Violation of these procedural requirements can lead to dismissal.
These sections provided the authority for the respondents to acquire the lands owned by the petitioners, forming the basis of the original acquisition proceedings.
The petitioners obtained stay orders but did not disclose them in the SLP. This conduct may be viewed as an abuse of process or laches, supporting the dismissal of the appeal on equitable grounds.

The petitioners filed the writ petition under this article, which guarantees the right to constitutional remedies. The court must determine if the High Court or Supreme Court has the jurisdiction to entertain this challenge to the statutory validity.

This is the primary provision challenged. It empowers the State Government to declare any substance as a poison via rules or notifications. The core legal issue is whether this delegation of legislative power is unguided and arbitrary.

The petitioners contend that the restrictions violate their right to carry on trade. This article guarantees the freedom to practice any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6).

The petitioners allege unjust and discriminatory application because the decision to include a substance as a poison is left to individual State Governments. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and prohibits arbitrary state action.

rules.provision: Rule 2(x) and Amendment Notification No. F. 10/44/72 fin. (G) dated 7.8.1973
rules.relevance: This specific rule and notification declared 'thinner' as a poison. The validity of this specific executive action under the parent Act is central to the dispute regarding the petitioners' product.

The case turns on whether Section 5 of the Poisons Act confers 'unguided, unchanneled, and arbitrary power' on the State Government. The court must apply principles regarding the limits of delegated legislation and the requirement of sufficient policy guidance in the parent statute.

This section allows regulation of possession in areas where poisoning is frequent. It provides context for the legislative intent and the scope of regulatory power, helping to determine if the power under Section 5 is reasonably connected to public safety.

This rule mandates storage and marking requirements. It illustrates the regulatory burden imposed on the petitioners and is relevant to assessing the reasonableness of the restrictions on their trade.

This provision allows the State to impose reasonable restrictions on the right to trade in the interest of the general public. The court must decide if the classification of 'thinner' as a poison constitutes a reasonable restriction.

rules.reference: Reasonableness Test for Restrictions on Trade
rules.relevance: The court must evaluate whether the restrictions imposed by the Act and Rules are proportionate to the objective of controlling traffic in poisons and protecting public health, balancing this against the petitioners' fundamental right to trade.

Defines the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal to inquire into and adjudicate industrial disputes, including the validity of termination orders and whether they constitute unfair labour practices or are colourable exercises of power.
Empowers the appropriate Government to refer industrial disputes to adjudication, which was the procedural basis for the Tribunal's involvement in this case.

rules.reference: Standing Orders of the Appellant's Saw Mill
rules.relevance: The specific contractual provision under which the appellant terminated Sankaran's services. The central issue is whether this rule allows termination without inquiry and whether it was invoked bona fide or as a colourable device to bypass disciplinary proceedings.

rules.case_name: Workmen of Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd.
rules.reference: Workmen of Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd.
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent establishing that while an employer may have the right to terminate under a standing order without assigning reasons, such power is not immune from judicial scrutiny if the termination is shown to be a colourable exercise of power or mala fide.

The legal principle that a power conferred by a standing order or statute cannot be used for a purpose other than that for which it was intended. Here, it addresses whether the termination was a sham to avoid a departmental inquiry for misconduct.

The principle that when an employer terminates a workman under a standing order without assigning reasons, the burden may shift to the employer to prove the bona fides of the action if the workman alleges it is a cover for misconduct-related dismissal.
Provides the statutory framework for certifying standing orders, which govern the conditions of service and termination rights of workmen in industrial establishments.

rules.case_name: Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of West Bengal
rules.reference: Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of West Bengal
rules.relevance: While primarily a tax case, it is often cited in Indian administrative law for the doctrine of colourable legislation/exercise of power, supporting the Tribunal's view that a power cannot be used indirectly to achieve what cannot be done directly.

Although termination under a standing order may not strictly require a domestic inquiry, the principle of natural justice and fair play suggests that if the employer initiates a charge sheet and suspension, they cannot arbitrarily abandon the inquiry to terminate under a different clause to prejudice the workman.
Deals with the finality of awards and the binding nature of the Tribunal's decision, which is relevant to the appeal challenging the Tribunal's award reinstating the workman.

This section empowers the Central Government to make rules for the better administration of the Army, including rules for the removal of officers. It is the enabling provision under which Rule 14 of the Army Rules, 1954 was framed, and its scope determines whether Rule 14 is intra vires.

This is the specific rule challenged in the appeal. It provides for the removal of an officer from service by the Central Government when a trial by Court Martial is deemed inexpedient. The core legal issue is whether this rule is validly made under the Army Act.

The respondent filed a petition under this article in the High Court challenging the removal order. The Supreme Court appeal arises from the High Court's exercise of jurisdiction under this article, making it procedurally relevant to the history of the case.

This section deals with the power to make rules for the better administration of the Army. It is often read in conjunction with Section 117 to determine the extent of rule-making power regarding disciplinary actions and removals.

The central legal question is whether Rule 14 is ultra vires the parent statute (Army Act, 1950). This principle dictates that any rule made under a statute must be within the scope of the authority conferred by that statute.

The facts state that the Chief of the Army Staff concluded a trial was 'inexpedient'. This legal concept justifies administrative removal instead of judicial trial in military contexts, and its validity under the Army Act is key to upholding Rule 14.

This section outlines the procedure for Courts Martial. The contrast between the judicial process under Section 121 and the administrative process under Rule 14 is central to determining if Rule 14 improperly bypasses statutory safeguards.

The Union of India filed an appeal by way of special leave to the Supreme Court. This article grants the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, order, or decree in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in India.

Although the primary issue is ultra vires, the facts mention Rao was called upon to submit his explanation. The extent to which natural justice applies to administrative removals under Rule 14, as opposed to Court Martial, is a relevant contextual principle.
This section deals with the publication of rules. It ensures that rules like Rule 14 are properly promulgated and have legal effect, supporting the procedural validity of the rule-making process.

rules.reference: Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973
rules.relevance: This section deleted Section 33 of the 1961 Act, thereby divesting the Panchayat Samiti of the statutory power to make appointments. This is central to determining whether the appellant's appointment as Head Clerk in 1975 was legally valid.

rules.reference: Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973
rules.relevance: This provision mandated that persons employed before April 1, 1973, continue in service on the same terms and conditions until absorbed. It defines the baseline status for absorption, raising the issue of whether 'terms and conditions' includes a post held after the authority lost appointment powers.

rules.reference: Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961
rules.relevance: This was the original provision under which the appellant was appointed as a clerk. Its deletion by the 1973 Amendment Act is the pivotal legal change affecting the validity of subsequent appointments by the Panchayat Samiti.

rules.reference: Principle of Validity of Appointment by Authority Lacking Statutory Power
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether an appointment or promotion made by a body after it has been statutorily divested of the power to make such appointments is valid. If the appointment is void ab initio, the appellant cannot claim absorption in that higher post.

This principle governs how employees of local bodies are absorbed into government service. It requires determining the substantive post held by the employee at the relevant time for absorption, contingent upon the legality of that post's creation and the employee's appointment to it.

The appellant originally filed a writ petition under this article in the High Court. The scope of judicial review under Article 226 regarding the validity of administrative appointments and statutory interpretation is relevant to the procedural history.
The appeal is filed by special leave under this article. It establishes the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear the appeal against the High Court's dismissal of the writ petition.

rules.reference: Interpretation of Saving Clauses in Statutes
rules.relevance: Section 14(4) acts as a saving clause. Legal principles regarding the interpretation of such clauses determine whether they preserve the status quo ante (clerk) or allow for subsequent changes in status, provided those changes are legally valid.

rules.reference: Effect of Retrospective Legislation on Service Matters
rules.relevance: Although the 1973 Act received assent in 1973, the deletion of Section 33 affected appointments made in 1975. Principles regarding whether the loss of power operates prospectively or renders subsequent acts void are relevant.

rules.reference: General Precedents on Absorption of Local Body Employees
rules.relevance: While specific case names are not provided in the brief, precedents establishing that absorption must be based on the substantive post held at the time of absorption, and that appointments made without statutory authority are invalid, are directly relevant.
This section empowers the Income Tax Officer to issue a notice for reassessment if income has escaped assessment. The core issue is whether the conditions precedent for issuing this notice were met.

This provision mandates that if a notice under Section 148 is issued after four years from the end of the relevant assessment year, the Income Tax Officer must record specific reasons for his belief that income has escaped assessment, and the Commissioner must be satisfied that it is a fit case. The facts highlight the lack of specific reasons and substantive satisfaction.

The appellant challenged the validity of the notice via a writ petition under this article, which empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights or for any other purpose. The High Court's dismissal is the subject of the appeal.
The appellant also invoked this article, which grants High Courts supervisory jurisdiction over all courts and tribunals within their territory, to challenge the proceedings.

rules.reference: Principle of Judicial Review of Administrative Satisfaction
rules.relevance: The principle that the satisfaction of the Commissioner under Section 151(2) must be based on relevant material and specific reasons recorded by the ITO, and cannot be a mere mechanical or formal act (such as writing 'yes'). The court must examine whether the satisfaction was bona fide and based on proper grounds.

rules.reference: Requirement of Specific Reasons for Reassessment
rules.relevance: The legal principle that vague references to 'bogus' transactions or 'name lenders' without specific material facts or investigation results do not constitute 'specific reasons' required by Section 151(2) to justify reassessment after the four-year period.

rules.case_name: Sital Prosad Mitter v. CIT
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the satisfaction of the Commissioner under Section 151(2) must be based on specific reasons recorded by the ITO and that the Commissioner's satisfaction is not a mere formality but a substantive requirement subject to judicial review.

rules.case_name: CIT v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills
rules.reference: CIT v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills
rules.relevance: This case is relevant for the proposition that the power of reassessment is an extraordinary power and must be exercised strictly within the limits prescribed by the statute, particularly regarding the recording of reasons and satisfaction.
Relevant to establish that the original assessment was completed, thereby triggering the need for Section 148/151 procedures to reopen the assessment, rather than a regular assessment process.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof in Reassessment Proceedings
rules.relevance: The principle that the burden lies on the Revenue to demonstrate that the statutory conditions for issuing a notice under Section 148 (specifically the satisfaction under Section 151(2)) have been fulfilled, especially when the notice is challenged on procedural grounds.

This is the primary procedural rule governing the substitution of parties in cases involving rights in respect of religious institutions or trusts. It determines whether the appeal could continue against Shiam Dass as the successor in interest to the office of Mahant, rather than abating due to the death of Som Dass.

This rule governs the general requirement to implead legal representatives of a deceased party within the prescribed limitation period. The High Court relied on the failure to comply with this rule to hold that the appeal abated.

This rule provides for the abatement of a suit or appeal if the legal representatives are not brought on record within the time prescribed by Order 22, Rule 3. This is the basis for the High Court's order of abatement.

This article prescribes the limitation period for applications for substitution of parties under Order 22 of the CPC. The appellant's failure to apply within this period is central to the abatement issue.

rules.reference: Nature of Rights in Religious Offices
rules.relevance: The legal principle that rights attached to a religious office (like Mahant) are not personal to the incumbent but attach to the office itself. This supports the argument that the successor steps into the shoes of the predecessor, potentially allowing continuation under Order 22, Rule 10 rather than abatement.

rules.case_name: Shri Lal Mahant v. Sarwan Singh
rules.reference: Shri Lal Mahant v. Sarwan Singh
rules.relevance: A leading precedent establishing that in disputes regarding religious institutions, the right to manage is attached to the office of the Mahant. This case is often cited to support the view that proceedings do not abate but continue against the successor.

rules.case_name: Gobind Das v. Ram Das
rules.relevance: This precedent discusses the application of Order 22, Rule 10 in the context of religious offices, holding that the successor in interest can be substituted to continue the litigation, preventing abatement.

This article grants the Supreme Court the power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, or final order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in India. It is the jurisdictional basis for the appellant's special leave appeal.

The distinction between cases where a right is personal (leading to abatement upon death) and cases where the right is attached to an office or status (allowing substitution of the successor). This principle is key to deciding if Order 22, Rule 10 overrides the general abatement rules.

This rule defines the circumstances under which a suit or appeal survives the death of a party. It sets the stage for determining whether the cause of action survived Som Dass's death, which is a prerequisite for applying Rule 10.

The specific provision challenged in the appeal. It prohibits licensed gold dealers from carrying on money lending or banking business on the security of gold articles unless authorized by the Administrator. The core legal question is whether this provision constitutes excessive delegation of legislative power.

The High Court struck down Section 28 on grounds of arbitrary and uncanalised discretion. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and prohibits arbitrary state action. The validity of delegated legislation is often tested against the standard of reasonableness and non-arbitrariness under Article 14.

The Act regulates the business of gold dealers. Restrictions on the right to practice any profession, trade, or business must be reasonable and not arbitrary. The challenge implies that the lack of guidelines for the Administrator's discretion makes the restriction unreasonable under Article 19.

rules.case_name: Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias v. Asst. Collector of Central Excise
rules.citation: Supreme Court decision cited by High Court
rules.reference: Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias v. Asst. Collector of Central Excise
rules.relevance: The High Court relied on this decision to strike down Section 28, drawing an analogy to Section 27(6) of the same Act which was struck down for excessive delegation. The Supreme Court must distinguish or apply this precedent to determine if Section 28 suffers from the same infirmity.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Excessive Delegation of Legislative Power
rules.relevance: The central legal issue is whether the legislature has abdicated its essential function by conferring uncanalised discretion on the Administrator. The principle requires that delegated power must be guided by sufficient policy, standards, or criteria to prevent arbitrariness.

rules.reference: Requirement of Guidelines and Policy in Delegated Legislation
rules.relevance: The Union of India argues that the objective and scheme of the Act provide sufficient guidance. This principle holds that if the parent Act lays down a clear policy, the executive's discretion to implement it may be valid even without explicit procedural safeguards like a hearing, provided the discretion is not arbitrary.

Referenced in the High Court's reasoning via the Harakchand case. Comparing the language and scope of discretion in Section 27(6) (struck down) with Section 28 (challenged) is crucial to determining if the same constitutional defect exists.

rules.reference: Distinction between Legislative and Executive Functions
rules.relevance: The court must determine if the power granted to the Administrator under Section 28 is legislative in nature (making law) or executive (applying law). Excessive delegation occurs when legislative power is transferred without adequate control.

rules.reference: Principle of Natural Justice in Administrative Discretion
rules.relevance: The High Court noted the lack of a requirement for hearing and reasons. While not always mandatory for every administrative decision, the absence of such safeguards can contribute to a finding of arbitrariness if the discretion is wide and affects fundamental rights.

The Union of India relies on the overall objective and scheme of the Act to argue that sufficient guidance exists. The court will examine the Act's purpose to see if it canalizes the Administrator's discretion sufficiently to save Section 28 from invalidity.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. It creates a presumption that if a public servant is in possession of property or money, it is presumed to be an illegal gratification unless the accused proves that it is a lawful income or gift. The appellant's appeal hinges on whether he successfully rebutted this presumption.

Defines the substantive offense of a public servant accepting or obtaining any gratification other than legal remuneration as a motive or reward for doing or forbearing to do any official act. The appellant was convicted under this section read with Section 5(2).
Provides for the punishment for the offenses defined in Section 5(1). The appellant was convicted under this section, making it relevant to the sentencing and conviction aspect of the appeal.

The appellant was also convicted under this section for taking gratification other than legal remuneration in connection with a public transaction. The High Court held no separate sentence was required, but the conviction under this section remains part of the judgment under appeal.

rules.reference: Standard of proof to rebut statutory presumption
rules.relevance: Relevant to determining whether the appellant's claim that the money was a 'return of a loan' or 'gift' met the required standard of proof to rebut the presumption under Section 4(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The court must assess if the explanation was probable and supported by evidence.

rules.reference: Admissibility and weight of phenolphthalein test
rules.relevance: The positive phenolphthalein test on the appellant's fingers is a key piece of circumstantial evidence linking him to the marked currency notes. Its relevance lies in corroborating the prosecution's case that the appellant handled the bribe money.

In corruption cases involving traps, the court examines the consistency of the prosecution witnesses (PW 1, PW 2, PW 6) and the recovery of the marked notes and the file. This principle guides the evaluation of whether the trap was genuine and the evidence reliable.

The appellant's defense rests on characterizing the transaction as a loan or gift. Legal principles regarding the nature of such transactions in the context of official acts are relevant to determine if the motive was corrupt or lawful.

Governs the powers of the Appellate Court to alter findings, sentences, or convictions. Relevant for the Supreme Court's authority to review the High Court's confirmation of the conviction and the decision on separate sentences.

rules.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram F. Meghe
rules.reference: State of Maharashtra v. Natu Ram F. Meghe
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent interpreting Section 4(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. It establishes that the presumption is not conclusive and can be rebutted by the accused proving that the money was a lawful gift or loan, but the burden of proof is on the accused to make out a probable case.

This is the primary statutory provision in dispute. The core issue is whether the Board of Revenue had jurisdiction under this section to exercise powers of superintendence and control to set aside orders of subordinate revenue courts when no appeal or revision was filed by the State.

The proceedings were initiated under this chapter to determine the ceiling area. Understanding the procedural framework of Chapter III B is necessary to interpret the scope of the Board's supervisory powers under Section 221 in the context of ceiling area determinations.

rules.reference: Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holding Act, 1973
rules.relevance: The Board of Revenue directed that the ceiling area be determined under the old law (1955 Act) rather than this new law. The applicability of the 1955 Act versus the 1973 Act is a foundational factual and legal premise for the jurisdictional analysis.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Jurisdictional Error vs. Error Apparent on Face of Record
rules.relevance: The Board set aside orders citing 'gross illegality'. The legal distinction between an error of jurisdiction (which may be corrected under superintendence powers) and an error of law/fact (which typically requires an appeal or revision) is central to deciding if the Board acted within its powers under Section 221.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice and Right to be Heard
rules.relevance: The Board disallowed the addition of evidence and set aside orders. The relevance lies in whether the exercise of superintendence powers under Section 221 requires affording the affected parties an opportunity of hearing before setting aside final orders, especially when the State is not a party to the appeal.

The writ petitions were filed under this article. The High Court's dismissal of the writs implies that the Board's action was not considered a violation of fundamental rights or a manifest excess of jurisdiction warranting writ intervention. This sets the context for the Special Leave Appeal.

The present appeal was filed via Special Leave under this article. The Supreme Court's jurisdiction to grant special leave depends on whether there is a substantial question of law or a grave miscarriage of justice regarding the interpretation of Section 221.

rules.reference: Separate Unit Status under Tenancy Laws
rules.relevance: The Sub Divisional Officer treated the father and minor son as two separate units. The Board found this to be 'gross illegality'. The legal definition of a 'unit' under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, is relevant to determine if the subordinate court's error was jurisdictional or merely factual/legal.

Procedural rules framed under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, may specify the manner in which the Board exercises its powers of superintendence and control, including whether it can act suo motu or only on reference.

rules.reference: General Precedents on Revenue Board's Superintendence Powers
rules.relevance: While specific case names are not provided in the brief, precedents interpreting similar 'superintendence and control' clauses in other state tenancy or revenue acts (e.g., distinguishing between appellate jurisdiction and supervisory jurisdiction) are likely relevant to interpret Section 221.

This is the primary procedural provision governing the recording of compromise decrees. The central issue is whether the court is bound to record the compromise despite one party's objection regarding non-payment of consideration, provided the compromise is lawful and genuine.

rules.case_name: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.reference: Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that a compromise decree is a decree in personam and binds the parties. It reinforces that if a compromise is lawful and genuine, the court should record it, and subsequent disputes regarding performance (like payment) are separate from the validity of the compromise itself.

Relevant to the second issue regarding the validity of alienations made by Sudarshan Gupta pendente lite. Under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, any transfer of property affected by a pending suit is void against the party in whose favor the suit is decided.

Codifies the doctrine of lis pendens. It determines whether the alienation of 81 acres by Sudarshan Gupta to third parties during the pendency of the suit is valid or void against the rights established by the compromise decree.

rules.case_name: K. Venugopala Pillai v. K. Venugopala Pillai
rules.reference: K. Venugopala Pillai v. K. Venugopala Pillai
rules.relevance: A key precedent establishing that a compromise decree is binding on the parties and their privies. It supports the view that the court should record the compromise if it is lawful, and the objection of non-payment does not invalidate the compromise itself but may give rise to a separate claim for damages or specific performance.

rules.case_name: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.reference: Raj Kumar v. Smt. Sushila Devi
rules.relevance: Holds that a compromise decree is a decree in personam and binds only the parties to it. This is relevant to determine the effect of the compromise on the alienees and whether the compromise extinguishes the title claims of the sons.
Relevant to the background facts concerning the validity of the wills and the adoption of K.V. Seshiah by Subbamma, which forms the basis of the competing title claims.

Relevant to Sudarshan Gupta's conduct of signing the compromise deed containing a clause acknowledging receipt of payment, and then later denying receipt. This principle may prevent him from taking a contrary position.

rules.case_name: Mohan Lal v. Kishan Lal
rules.relevance: Discusses the scope of Order 23 Rule 3 and the court's duty to examine whether the compromise is lawful and genuine. It supports the proposition that minor irregularities or disputes over consideration do not necessarily preclude recording the compromise.

Relevant to the alienees' claim of possession for more than three years. While three years is short for adverse possession, this section bars suits on rights acquired by possession after the expiration of the period of limitation, which may be argued by the alienees if they claim title by possession.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Dedication and Nucleus Theory
rules.relevance: Central to the appeal. The appellants argue that the properties belong to the Math because they were acquired from a 'nucleus' of dedicated property. The court must determine if the funds used (inherited personal wealth) retain their character as personal property or if the mere use of Math-associated funds creates a presumption of dedication to the deity.

rules.reference: Personal Property of Mahant vs. Math Property
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is distinguishing between property held by a Mahant in his personal capacity versus property held in trust for the Math. The facts highlight that the predecessor was a Dashnami Sanyasi who accumulated personal wealth, raising the question of whether such wealth remains personal upon succession.

Mahant Shivshanker Yati obtained a succession certificate for the fixed deposits inherited from Mahant Shivpher Yati. This statutory act supports the finding that the funds were treated as personal estate subject to succession laws, rather than inalienable Math property.

Mahant Shivshanker Yati executed a will in 1956 bequeathing the Amauli properties to Uma Shanker Yati. The validity and effect of this will depend on whether the testator had the legal capacity to dispose of the property as his own, which hinges on the classification of the property as personal.

In Hindu religious institutions, there is often a presumption that property acquired by a Mahant belongs to the Math. The High Court rejected this presumption based on the source of funds (personal inheritance) and revenue records. The appeal challenges this rejection, requiring analysis of when the presumption applies and when it is rebutted.

rules.reference: Estoppel and Conduct in Tax Proceedings
rules.relevance: The High Court noted that the Mahant's claim in tax proceedings that the properties belonged to the Math was made solely to escape personal tax liability. This principle of estoppel or inconsistent conduct is relevant to determining the true nature of the title and the Mahant's intent.

rules.provision: Section 35 (Relevancy of Entries in Public Documents)
rules.reference: Rules of Evidence regarding Revenue Records
rules.relevance: The revenue records listed the properties in the name of Mahant Shivshanker Yati, not the Math. Under the Indian Evidence Act, entries in public records made in the discharge of official duty are relevant to prove the fact stated, supporting the finding of personal ownership.

Mahant Shivpher Yati was a Dashnami Sanyasi. Legal precedents often distinguish between the property of a Sanyasi who has renounced the world (which may vest in the Math) and personal assets accumulated before renunciation or through specific personal inheritance, which may remain personal.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof in Dedication Cases
rules.relevance: The plaintiffs bear the burden to prove that the properties were dedicated to the deity. The High Court found the income from dedicated properties insufficient to generate the surplus for purchase, shifting the focus to the source of funds. The appeal requires reviewing whether the plaintiffs met this burden.

rules.provision: Order XLI, Rule 31 (Appeal from Findings of Fact)
rules.relevance: The present appeal challenges the High Court's findings of fact regarding the source of funds and the nature of the property. The appellate court must determine if these findings are perverse or based on no evidence, as appellate courts generally do not interfere with concurrent findings of fact unless they are erroneous in law.

rules.reference: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: This is the primary substantive provision defining the offense of 'relinquishment of tenancy' for consideration. The central legal issue is whether the appellant's actions fall within the definition of relinquishment under this section.

rules.reference: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: This is the penal provision under which the appellant was convicted. It prescribes the punishment for contravening Section 19(1). The appeal challenges the validity of this conviction.

rules.reference: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: The appellant was also charged under this section, which typically prohibits the assignment or sub-letting of premises without permission. The appellant's defense relies on characterizing the transaction as an assignment rather than a relinquishment, making this section contextually relevant to the distinction between the two concepts.

rules.reference: Distinction between Assignment and Relinquishment of Tenancy
rules.relevance: The core legal principle to be applied is the distinction between 'assignment' (transfer of interest) and 'relinquishment' (giving up possession/interest to the landlord or a third party in a manner that extinguishes the tenancy). The court must determine if handing over vacant possession to a third party constitutes relinquishment.

rules.reference: Interpretation of 'Relinquishment' in Rent Control Legislation
rules.relevance: The court must interpret the term 'relinquishment' in the context of rent control laws. The principle involves determining whether the intent and effect of the transaction were to surrender the tenancy rights entirely, thereby triggering the prohibition against taking consideration for such surrender.

rules.case_name: W.H. King v. Mulchand Kodumal Bhatia
rules.reference: W.H. King v. Mulchand Kodumal Bhatia
rules.relevance: This is the specific case being appealed. The Supreme Court's decision in this matter established the precedent regarding whether a transaction involving payment for vacant possession constitutes relinquishment under Section 19 of the Bombay Rents Act.

rules.reference: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Section 10 generally deals with the control of rents and the rights of tenants. While not the specific penal section, it provides the statutory framework for tenancy rights and restrictions on transfer, which informs the interpretation of Sections 18 and 19.

rules.reference: Substance over Form in Rent Control Transactions
rules.relevance: Courts often look at the substance of the transaction rather than its form. If the effect of the 'assignment' is that the original tenant surrenders all rights and possession for a lump sum, it may be treated as a relinquishment prohibited by Section 19, regardless of the label used in the document.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (or 1898 as applicable)
rules.relevance: Procedural rule governing the right to appeal against a conviction by a Presidency Magistrate to the High Court and subsequently to the Supreme Court. This establishes the jurisdictional basis for the appeal.

The principle that receiving money specifically for 'vacant possession' is the hallmark of a relinquishment transaction under rent control laws, distinguishing it from a lawful assignment where the tenant transfers their interest but the tenancy continues.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that cancellation of recruitment is a drastic step and should be resorted to only when the error is so fundamental that it vitiates the entire process. It distinguishes between errors affecting the merit list versus those affecting only the call for interview, suggesting that re-calling the correct candidates is often a preferable remedy to total cancellation.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.reference: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
rules.relevance: Reinforces the view that if the error is curable (e.g., wrong candidates called for interview due to clerical error), the remedy is to correct the list and call the rightful candidates, rather than cancelling the entire examination, provided the integrity of the written exam remains intact.

rules.reference: Article 309 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Governs the recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the Union or a State. It empowers the State to make rules for recruitment, implying that the process must be fair, transparent, and in accordance with the established rules, which the Commission failed to follow due to the data entry error.

rules.reference: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of laws. Arbitrary cancellation of a valid written examination due to a correctable administrative error may be challenged as arbitrary and violative of the legitimate expectations of the candidates who performed well.

rules.reference: Article 320 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: Deals with the functions of Public Service Commissions. While the Commission has the authority to conduct examinations, its actions must be judicially reviewable if they are arbitrary or violate the principles of natural justice, especially when the error is technical and curable.

Candidates who have cleared the written examination have a legitimate expectation to be considered for the next stage. Canceling the entire process without exploring curative measures (like re-calling the correct candidates) defeats this expectation and is legally unsustainable unless the error is incurable.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Proportionality in Administrative Action
rules.relevance: The remedy chosen by the administration (total cancellation) must be proportionate to the error committed (data entry mistake in interview list). Total cancellation is a disproportionate response to a clerical error that can be rectified by correcting the interview list.

rules.case_name: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.reference: Rajesh Kumar v. State of Haryana
rules.relevance: Holds that if the error is in the preparation of the merit list or call letters, and the written exam is valid, the court can direct the authority to prepare a fresh merit list or call the correct candidates, rather than cancelling the entire recruitment process.

rules.reference: The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission (Conduct of Business) Rules
rules.relevance: These rules govern the conduct of the UP PSC. While specific sections are not cited, the general framework requires the Commission to act fairly and in accordance with the recruitment rules. The error in data entry likely violated the procedural fairness mandated by these rules.

rules.case_name: S. R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: S. R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Discusses the scope of judicial review in recruitment matters. It emphasizes that while courts do not interfere with the merits of selection, they do intervene when the process is vitiated by illegality, irrationality, or procedural impropriety, such as a fundamental error in the call list that affects the rights of eligible candidates.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the appellant claimed maintenance. The central issue is whether a divorced wife who has not remarried falls within the definition of 'wife' entitled to maintenance under this section.

This provision allows for the modification or cancellation of maintenance orders if the wife has remarried or, in the case of a divorced wife, if she has received the whole amount of maintenance allowed by any decree or order. The issue is whether the prior consent decree and mehar payment constitute such a receipt that extinguishes the right to further maintenance.

This provision states that no wife shall be entitled to receive maintenance if she is living in adultery, or if she refuses to live with her husband without sufficient reason. The issue involves the burden of proof regarding whether the wife was living separately by mutual consent or without sufficient reason.

rules.case_name: Danial Latifi & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Danial Latifi & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: This is the landmark Supreme Court judgment interpreting Section 125 CrPC in the context of Muslim law. It held that a divorced Muslim woman who has not remarried is entitled to maintenance under Section 125 until she remarries, and that 'mahr' and 'iddat' money do not automatically extinguish this statutory right if they are insufficient for her maintenance.

rules.case_name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
rules.reference: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
rules.relevance: This earlier landmark precedent established that a divorced Muslim woman is entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. It is highly relevant as it forms the basis for the appellant's claim and was the subject of subsequent legislative amendments and judicial interpretations like Danial Latifi.

The legal principle that the burden lies on the husband to prove that the wife is living in adultery or refusing to live with him without sufficient reason. If the husband fails to prove this, the wife is entitled to maintenance. This addresses the issue of whether the husband must prove the wife was not living separately by mutual consent.

The principle that Section 125 CrPC is a summary provision intended to prevent vagrancy and destitution, and its scope is not limited by personal laws. Therefore, personal law concepts like 'mahr' do not necessarily override the statutory obligation to provide maintenance if the wife is unable to maintain herself.

Specifically defines 'wife' to include a woman who has been divorced by, or has obtained any divorce from, her husband and has not remarried. This is the specific clause determining the appellant's eligibility.

rules.case_name: Emayambal v. Shanmugham
rules.relevance: While predating the 1973 Code, this case (and similar precedents under the 1898 Code) established that a divorced wife who has not remarried is entitled to maintenance. It supports the interpretation that the status of 'divorcee' does not bar maintenance claims if the wife is unable to maintain herself.

The principle that a private agreement or consent decree regarding property or mehar does not necessarily waive the statutory right to maintenance under Section 125 unless it explicitly and effectively provides for maintenance equivalent to what the court would award. The court must examine if the mehar/iddat money was sufficient for her maintenance.

This is the primary statutory instrument defining the Scheduled Castes for West Bengal. The specific phrase 'Sunri excluding Saha' in Item 40 is the central subject of interpretation to determine if the appellant is eligible to contest the reserved seat.

Section 8 mandates that a candidate for a seat reserved for Scheduled Castes must be a member of a Scheduled Caste. This section establishes the legal consequence of failing to meet the caste requirement, i.e., the election is void.

This section provides the ground for declaring an election void if the candidate elected was not entitled to be so elected, specifically addressing the issue of eligibility regarding caste status in reserved constituencies.

This section outlines the procedure for determining the result of an election petition. It is relevant to the second appeal (No. 1149) concerning whether the respondent should be declared elected in place of the appellant if the appellant's election is set aside.

rules.reference: Principle of Interpretation of Exclusionary Clauses in Statutory Orders
rules.relevance: The core legal issue is whether 'excluding Saha' refers to a surname or a distinct sub-caste. The principle that statutory exclusions must be interpreted based on legislative intent and social reality (distinct caste identity) rather than mere nomenclature is central to the decision.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof in Election Petitions
rules.relevance: The facts state the respondent failed to prove the appellant belonged to a distinct 'Saha' sub-caste. The legal principle regarding the burden of proof on the petitioner to establish that the candidate does not belong to the scheduled caste is relevant.

Article 341 empowers the President to specify Scheduled Castes. It establishes the legal framework under which the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 was issued, giving it constitutional status.

This section deals with the rejection of nominations. It is relevant to the procedural history where the Returning Officer initially rejected the objection, and the subsequent challenge to that decision in the election petition.

rules.reference: Preventive Detention Act (State Act applicable in Bihar/Jharkhand region, e.g., Bihar Maintenance of Public Order Act or similar)
rules.relevance: This is the specific statutory provision under which the District Magistrate passed the detention order. The validity of the order depends on whether the conditions precedent under this section were satisfied, particularly regarding the necessity of detention.

Article 22(5) mandates that the detenu be furnished with the grounds of detention and given the earliest opportunity to make a representation against it. This is central to the procedural fairness challenge regarding the service of the order and the consideration of the representation.

Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty. Preventive detention is a deprivation of liberty, and any order must satisfy the requirements of legality, reasonableness, and fairness under this article.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Lallu Singh
rules.reference: State of Bihar v. Lallu Singh
rules.relevance: This is a landmark precedent establishing that the detaining authority must apply its mind to the 'imminent prospect of release' of the detenu. If the detenu is already in judicial custody and there is no imminent prospect of release, the detention order may be vitiated for lack of necessity. This directly addresses the appellant's core contention.

rules.case_name: Rajbali Pandey v. State of Bihar
rules.reference: Rajbali Pandey v. State of Bihar
rules.relevance: Reinforces the principle that preventive detention is not a punishment but a preventive measure. Therefore, if the detenu is already in custody and poses no immediate threat to public order upon release (or if release is not imminent), the detention order lacks the necessary nexus with public order.

The detaining authority must independently apply its mind to the facts, including the detenu's current custody status. The failure to consider the 'imminent prospect of release' constitutes a failure of application of mind, rendering the order invalid.

If a person is already in judicial custody, serving a preventive detention order is futile unless there is a clear and imminent prospect of their release from judicial custody. The order must be based on the likelihood of the detenu being at large and causing harm.

rules.case_name: A.K. Roy v. Union of India
rules.reference: A.K. Roy v. Union of India
rules.relevance: While primarily about the validity of the Act, this case discusses the scope of preventive detention and the necessity of the detaining authority's satisfaction. It supports the view that detention must be necessary for public order, not merely punitive or redundant.

The detention order stated the appellant was 'likely to be enlarged on bail'. The rules governing bail in non-bailable offenses (like murder) are relevant to assess whether the detaining authority's assumption of 'imminent release' was reasonable or speculative.

rules.reference: High Court of Patna Writ Jurisprudence
rules.relevance: The High Court dismissed the writ petition without a speaking order. Precedents regarding the High Court's duty to pass reasoned orders in writ petitions challenging detention (under Article 226) are relevant to challenge the procedural propriety of the High Court's dismissal.

This section governs the grant of licences to run cinematograph theatres. It is central to determining who holds the legal right to operate the theatre and whether the licence is an individual asset or partnership property, which dictates the scope of the District Magistrate's authority.

This section empowers the District Magistrate to suspend the exhibition of films if the licence conditions are violated, such as exhibition by persons other than the licensee. It is the statutory basis for the impugned suspension order.

rules.reference: Principles of Natural Justice (Audi Alteram Partem)
rules.relevance: The core issue is whether the District Magistrate violated natural justice by suspending the licence without hearing the partnership firm, which claimed an interest in the licence. This principle determines the procedural validity of the administrative order.

This section defines the nature of partnership and the rights of partners. It is relevant to determine if the licence, granted in Ved Gupta's name, became partnership property by conduct or agreement, thereby giving the firm a locus standi to challenge the suspension.

This article empowers the High Court to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. It is the jurisdictional basis for the writ petition filed by the firm and the subsequent Letters Patent Appeal.

This rule governs appeals from orders, including those passed in writ proceedings or interlocutory orders. It is relevant to the procedural history of the Letters Patent Appeal filed by Ved Gupta against the Division Bench's decision.

The case hinges on whether the District Magistrate had the jurisdiction to act against the firm when the licence was in Ved Gupta's name. This principle addresses the limits of administrative power vis-a-vis civil rights and property interests.

rules.reference: Res Judicata / Finality of Previous Determinations
rules.relevance: The facts state that the Supreme Court had previously dismissed challenges to Ved Gupta being the sole licensee. This principle is relevant to determine if the firm is barred from re-litigating the ownership of the licence or if the new suspension order is a distinct administrative action.

This section outlines the rights of partners, including the right to take part in the conduct of the business. It supports the firm's claim that they had an interest in the operation of the theatre and thus a right to be heard before suspension.

This principle determines who has the legal standing to challenge an administrative order. It is crucial in deciding whether the partnership firm, despite not being the named licensee, had sufficient interest to demand a hearing under natural justice.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the revision application was filed. The central issue is whether the High Court had jurisdiction under this section to interfere with an interlocutory order regarding the admissibility of evidence and the application of res judicata.

This section defines the doctrine of res judicata. The dispute centers on whether the consent decree in the previous suit operated as res judicata to bar the defendants from challenging the nature of the agreement in the subsequent suit.

rules.reference: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: This provision determined the jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes to try the suit. It establishes the procedural context in which the trial judge's order was made.

The legal principle that revision jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC is limited to cases where the lower court has exercised jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity, and generally does not extend to correcting errors of law or fact in interlocutory orders unless they affect the merits of the case or cause irreparable injury.

The principle regarding whether a consent decree operates as res judicata. Specifically, whether matters not explicitly decided but necessary for the consent decree to be effective are barred from re-litigation.

This section prohibits oral evidence to contradict the terms of a written contract. The trial judge allowed oral evidence to explain the terms, raising the question of whether this was barred by Section 92, which was one of the preliminary issues Filmistan sought to raise.

The principle that revision is not an appeal and that high courts should not interfere with interlocutory orders (such as those permitting cross-examination questions) unless the order is of a jurisdictional nature or causes grave injustice that cannot be remedied later.
This rule governs the compromise of suits and the recording of consent decrees. It is relevant to determining the legal effect and finality of the consent decree passed in Suit No. 149 of 1960.

The principle of estoppel, which Filmistan argued barred the defendants from challenging the nature of the agreement. This is closely related to res judicata but focuses on the parties' conduct and the decree's effect on their rights.
This section defines estoppel. It is relevant to the argument that the defendants were estopped from denying the nature of the transaction based on the previous consent decree.
Defines 'public trust' as a trust created for public purposes and charitable purposes, which is the central statutory definition required to determine if the Sansthan falls under the Act's purview.
The provision under which the application for registration was filed; determines the procedural basis for the Assistant Charity Commissioner's jurisdiction to register the trust.

rules.case_name: Shri Vithal Sukhamai Sansthan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.reference: Shri Vithal Sukhamai Sansthan v. State of Maharashtra
rules.relevance: This is the specific Supreme Court judgment deciding the appeal described in the facts. It establishes the legal test for distinguishing between public and private trusts based on the nature of the dedication and public access.

The core legal principle applied to determine if a religious institution is a public trust. It holds that if property is dedicated to a deity for public worship and the public has a right to enter, it constitutes a public trust regardless of the founder's initial intent or private management structures.

rules.reference: Substance over Form in Trust Classification
rules.relevance: Relevant to interpreting the 1869 Varaspatra and 1897 Vyavasthapatra. The principle dictates that the use of terms like 'Malaki' (owner) does not negate public trust status if the actual usage and dedication are for public religious purposes.

rules.case_name: Raghunath Prasad v. State of U.P.
rules.reference: Raghunath Prasad v. State of U.P.
rules.relevance: A leading precedent often cited in such disputes to establish that the character of a trust is determined by the nature of the dedication and the rights of the public, not merely by the mode of management or succession rules.

Supports the argument that once a property is dedicated to a deity for public worship (as evidenced by the 1863 Sanad and subsequent gift deeds), it ceases to be private property and cannot be reclaimed as such by the founder's heirs.
Defines 'charitable purpose' to include religious purposes, which is essential to classify the Sansthan's activities (temple worship, festivals) as falling within the scope of the Act.

rules.reference: Evidence of Public Access as Determinative
rules.relevance: Relates to the oral evidence of Ramkrishna Deshpande. The principle holds that unrestricted public access for Darshan and the support of devotees are strong indicators of a public trust, overriding private ownership claims.

rules.case_name: Gobind Dayal v. State of Punjab
rules.reference: Gobind Dayal v. State of Punjab
rules.relevance: Relevant for the interpretation of historical documents (Sanads, Varaspatras) in the context of trust law, emphasizing that the intent of the founder must be read in light of the actual dedication and public usage.

This article grants the High Court the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territory, including the power to issue orders staying proceedings. The validity and scope of the stay order issued under this article are central to determining if contempt occurred.

Defines 'civil contempt' as the wilful disobedience to any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court. The core issue is whether the Panchayat's actions constituted 'wilful' disobedience given the defective evidence of the stay.
Governs the punishment for contempt, including fines and imprisonment. This section is relevant to the appellate review of the sentence imposed by the High Court.

rules.case_name: In re: Arundhati Roy
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that contempt jurisdiction is meant to protect the administration of justice, not to punish for the sake of punishment. It emphasizes that disobedience must be wilful and deliberate, which is key to assessing the Panchayat's intent.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagwanji
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent regarding contempt of court, establishing that the test for contempt is whether the act was a deliberate disobedience of a clear and unambiguous order. It helps determine if the informal affidavit provided sufficient notice to make the disobedience 'wilful'.

States that when the terms of a contract, grant, or other disposition of property have been reduced to writing, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such contract or grant other than the document itself. This is relevant to the argument that the unsworn, informal document was insufficient proof of the High Court's order.

Deals with the proof of signatures and handwriting. While less central, it relates to the authenticity of the document presented. More importantly, the lack of proper authentication (not sworn before an authorized person) undermines its evidentiary value.

The legal principle that for civil contempt to be established, the disobedience must be wilful. If the Panchayat reasonably believed the stay was not in effect due to the defective nature of the affidavit (unsworn, no date, no copy of telegram), their action may not be considered wilful.
Defines the jurisdiction and powers of the Nyaya Panchayat. Relevant to understand the procedural context in which the Panchayat was operating and their duty to comply with superior court orders.

rules.case_name: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
rules.reference: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Discusses the scope of Article 227 and the High Court's power to stay proceedings. It provides context on the binding nature of such stay orders on subordinate bodies like Nyaya Panchayats.

This is the primary constitutional provision granting Parliament the power to make laws prescribing residence requirements for appointments in a State. The central legal issue is the interpretation of whether 'State' in this clause allows for residence requirements within a specific part of a State.

rules.reference: The Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957
rules.relevance: This is the specific Act of Parliament enacted under Article 16(3) that empowers the State Government to make rules regarding residence requirements. The petitioners challenge the validity of this Act as ultra vires the Constitution.

rules.reference: The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959
rules.relevance: These rules, made under the 1957 Act, specifically required continuous residence in the Telengana area for fifteen years. The validity of these rules depends on the interpretation of the enabling Act and Article 16(3).

Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. The petitioners argue that the residence requirement violates this general principle of equality, making the interpretation of the exception in Article 16(3) crucial.

Although enacted later (1985), this article specifically addresses safeguards for certain areas in the State of Andhra Pradesh regarding public employment. It is highly relevant as it reflects the constitutional recognition of the need for such safeguards, supporting the respondents' argument that Parliament has the power to prescribe such requirements.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. N. Swamy
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh v. N. Swamy
rules.relevance: This is the specific Supreme Court case corresponding to the facts provided. It directly decided the issue of whether Parliament could prescribe residence requirements for a part of a State under Article 16(3).

The legal principle concerning whether the term 'State' in Article 16(3) refers to the entire geographical entity or can be interpreted to allow for regional safeguards within a State is the core interpretive question.

Article 16(4) allows for reservations for backward classes. While distinct from residence requirements, it is often cited in comparative analysis to determine the scope of exceptions to equality in public employment under Article 16.

This Act led to the formation of the unified State of Andhra Pradesh by merging Andhra and Telengana. The historical context of this merger and the political agreements (Telengana Safeguards) are relevant to understanding the legislative intent behind the residence rules.
The petitioners' claim that the Act and Rules are ultra vires the Constitution relies on this principle. The court must determine if the legislation exceeds the powers granted by Article 16(3).
The primary substantive charge under which all accused were convicted for murder. The appeal challenges the sustainability of this conviction, particularly for Pandurang.
Central to the defense of Pandurang, who argues that without evidence of common intention or prior concert, his conviction for murder cannot be sustained under Section 302 read with Section 34.

The appellants specifically argued that the death sentence required the concurrence of two judges under this section. The procedural history involves a difference of opinion in the High Court, making the interpretation of this provision regarding sentencing crucial.
Defines the offense of murder. The court must determine if the acts of the accused (striking with axes/sticks) fall under the clauses of Section 300 to attract the punishment under Section 302.

rules.reference: Principle of Common Intention vs. Common Object
rules.relevance: Relevant to distinguishing the liability of Pandurang (different caste, no prior concert) from the other accused. The court must apply principles determining when individual acts can be attributed to a group under Section 34.

rules.reference: Evaluation of Eyewitness Testimony and Identification
rules.relevance: The conviction relies on the testimony of Rasika Bai and Subhana. The court must apply legal principles regarding the reliability of eyewitness accounts, especially concerning the identification of specific blows inflicted by specific accused.

rules.reference: Corroboration of Eyewitness Testimony with Medical Evidence
rules.relevance: The court must reconcile the eyewitness account of the blows (cheek, head, neck) with the medical evidence (lacerated wound on face, incised wounds on scalp/neck) to establish the cause of death and the role of each accused.

rules.reference: Effect of Delay and Omission in FIR
rules.relevance: The defense argued concoction based on the FIR not naming the accused. The court applied the principle that such omissions can be explained by 'rustic simplicity' and lack of immediate knowledge, which is a key evidentiary principle in Indian criminal law.

Governs the procedure when judges of a High Court differ in opinion. The case was referred to a third judge (P.J. Reddy) under this mechanism, which is relevant to the procedural validity of the High Court's final order.

The High Court's jurisdiction to entertain the appeal and the subsequent refusal of leave to appeal to the Supreme Court falls under the writ jurisdiction and appellate powers defined in the Constitution.

rules.reference: The Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955
rules.relevance: This is the central statutory provision defining 'newspaper' as 'any printed periodical work containing public news or comments on public news'. The appeal hinges entirely on whether the respondent's law reports fall within this definition.

rules.reference: The Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955
rules.relevance: This section empowers the Central Government to constitute Tribunals to fix or revise wages for working journalists, establishing the procedural basis for the Palekar Award.

rules.reference: The Working Journalists and Other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955
rules.relevance: This section relates to the constitution of Tribunals for non-journalist newspaper employees, further establishing the statutory framework under which the wage fixation occurred.

rules.reference: Principle of Statutory Interpretation: Literal and Purposive Construction
rules.relevance: The court must interpret the phrase 'public news or comments on public news' in Section 2(b). The principle requires determining if legal news and commentary constitute 'public news' in the ordinary sense intended by the legislature.

rules.reference: Principle of Beneficial Construction of Labour Welfare Legislation
rules.relevance: As a social welfare statute regulating conditions of service, the Act should be interpreted liberally to cover employees who perform journalistic functions, unless explicitly excluded.
The court must determine if law reports, published at regular intervals, qualify as 'printed periodical work' under the Act, distinct from one-time publications or books.
The core factual issue is whether reports of court judgments and legal analysis constitute 'public news' or 'comments on public news' as opposed to specialized professional literature.
Procedural rule governing appeals from decrees or orders, relevant to the procedural history of the appeal from the High Court's judgment.
The appellants filed a special leave appeal, which is exercised by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution, granting jurisdiction to hear the appeal against the High Court's decision.

rules.reference: Principle of Precedent and Stare Decisis
rules.relevance: The court will consider whether previous interpretations of 'newspaper' under this Act or similar labour laws bind or guide the current determination regarding law reports.

Central to the appellants' argument that the Act provides a complete code for sickness benefits and bars similar benefits under other enactments or awards, thereby precluding the Tribunal from awarding additional paid sick leave.
Cited by workmen to argue that ESIC benefits are inadequate because they exclude benefits for the first two days of sickness, justifying the need for additional paid sick leave from the employer.
Defines the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal to adjudicate disputes regarding terms and conditions of service, including leave benefits, which is the basis for the Tribunal's award.

rules.case_name: Alembic Glass Industries Ltd. v. Workmen
rules.citation: 1979 Lab IC 1085 (Gujarat) or similar companion appeal citation
rules.reference: Alembic Glass Industries Ltd. v. Workmen
rules.relevance: The specific case in question; the Supreme Court's decision in this companion appeal establishes the precedent on whether ESIC benefits preclude the award of paid sick leave by Industrial Tribunals.

rules.case_name: Jyoti Limited v. Workmen
rules.citation: Companion appeal to Alembic Glass Industries
rules.relevance: The specific case in question; addresses the issue of retrospective effect of the award from January 1, 1975, and the validity of the Tribunal's jurisdiction in granting such benefits.
Legal principle determining whether statutory benefits (ESIC) are sufficient to meet the workmen's needs or if they are merely contributory, allowing for supplementary benefits via industrial awards.

Determines whether the Employees' State Insurance Act is intended to substitute all other forms of sickness relief or merely supplement them, which dictates the Tribunal's power to award additional leave.
Governs the finality and binding nature of Tribunal awards, relevant to the challenge against the legality and enforceability of the awards granted.
Relevant to the Jyoti Limited issue regarding whether an Industrial Tribunal can award benefits with retrospective effect to a date prior to the award, specifically January 1, 1975.
Details the specific sickness benefits provided under the Act, which must be compared against the awarded leave to determine if the statutory scheme is exhaustive.

This is the primary statutory provision governing the devolution of interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property upon the death of a coparcener. The core legal dispute centers on the interpretation of Explanation 1 to this section regarding the calculation of the deceased's interest.

The specific explanation to Section 6 states that the interest of a deceased coparcener shall be deemed to be that share which would have been allotted to him if a partition had taken place immediately before his death. The appeal hinges on whether this 'deemed interest' includes the widow's own notional share in the joint family property.

rules.case_name: Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum
rules.reference: Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum
rules.relevance: This is the actual case described in the facts. The Supreme Court's judgment in this matter established the 'notional partition' doctrine, holding that the widow is entitled to her own share in the coparcenary property in addition to her share in the deceased husband's interest, thereby validating the 7/24th share claim.

rules.case_name: Rangubai Lalji v. Laxman Lalji
rules.relevance: Cited by the Bombay High Court in the procedural history to support the plaintiff's claim for a 7/24th share. It represents the view that the widow's share includes her own notional interest in the joint family property.

rules.case_name: Shiramabai Bhimgonda v. Kalgonda
rules.relevance: Cited by the trial court to limit the plaintiff's share to 1/24th. This authority represents the opposing view that the widow's share is restricted only to her share in the deceased husband's notional interest, excluding her own potential share in the coparcenary.

The legal principle applied to determine the extent of the deceased coparcener's interest. It requires imagining a partition immediately preceding death to ascertain the shares of all members, including the widow, to correctly apply Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act.

Governs the general scheme of succession for male Hindus dying intestate. While Section 6 is specific to coparcenary property, Section 8 provides the context for the widow's status as a Class I heir, relevant to understanding her entitlement to the husband's share.

Background legal principle defining the nature of joint family property and the rights of members. It establishes that while a widow is not a coparcener, she has a right to maintenance and a share in the partition of joint family property, which is central to the calculation of her 7/24th share.

rules.case_name: State Bank of India vs Prakash Chand Mehra
rules.reference: State Bank of India vs Prakash Chand Mehra
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court's interpretation of similar provisions in the Sastry Award is directly relevant as the Desai Award required workmen to first be fitted into the scales of the Sastry Award. This precedent establishes the judicial approach to interpreting fitment and ceiling clauses in bank industrial awards.

rules.reference: National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award of June 1962 (Desai Award)
rules.relevance: This is the primary instrument under dispute. Specifically, the interplay between Clause (ii) (ceiling on adjusted basic pay) and Clause (iv)(d) (grant of two further annual increments) determines the appellants' liability.
Provides the statutory basis for the reference to the National Industrial Tribunal and the binding nature of the Tribunal's Award on the parties involved.
Defines the 'Award' and its finality, which is central to the enforcement of the Labour Court's order interpreting the Award.
Establishes the binding nature of the Award on the parties to the dispute, preventing the bank from unilaterally ignoring the interpretation of the increments.
Defines the jurisdiction of the Labour Court to determine disputes regarding the interpretation and implementation of awards.
Relates to the publication of awards and their enforceability as decrees of a civil court, relevant for the execution of the pay fixation order.
Governs the modification and withdrawal of awards, relevant if the bank argues for a reinterpretation that effectively modifies the original intent of the Tribunal.
Defines the period of operation of an award, ensuring the temporal validity of the Desai Award's provisions regarding the years 1960 and 1961.
A general principle of statutory and award interpretation requiring that conflicting clauses (ceiling vs. increments) be read together to give effect to both, rather than rendering one nugatory.

Defines the jurisdiction of the Central Administrative Tribunal to adjudicate disputes regarding conditions of service and disciplinary proceedings of government servants, which is the foundational basis for the CAT's intervention.

Grants the Tribunal the powers of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including the power to modify penalties if the Tribunal is satisfied that the penalty imposed is excessive or disproportionate to the misconduct.

Empowers the Tribunal to pass such orders as it deems fit, including modifying the penalty awarded by the competent authority, provided the findings of fact are not interfered with unless they are perverse.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tarsem Singh
rules.relevance: A landmark precedent establishing that the CAT has the power to modify the penalty if it finds the penalty imposed by the competent authority to be excessive or disproportionate, even if the findings of guilt are upheld.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.reference: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that while the Tribunal can interfere with the penalty, it should not act as an appellate court on facts unless the findings are perverse. It clarifies the scope of judicial review in disciplinary matters.
The specific rules under which the departmental proceedings were initiated and the charges of misconduct (fraud, impersonation) were framed against the respondent.

Provision under which the pending writ petition in the High Court was transferred to the Central Administrative Tribunal, establishing the Tribunal's jurisdiction over the matter.

Relevant to determine the legal status of the firm after Amarchand's death. Section 37 deals with the dissolution of a firm by the death of a partner and the rights of the deceased partner's legal representatives, which informs whether the receipts are income or capital.

Deals with the assessment of a deceased person for the year in which they died. Comparing Section 24A with Section 24B helps in interpreting the legislative intent regarding the assessment of post-death receipts.

Provides the defense of 'fair and accurate report of judicial proceedings' or 'fair criticism' of judicial action. States that no contempt is committed if the person shows that they had no reason to believe that there were reasonable grounds for believing that the matter alleged was true. rules.case_name: In re: Arundhati Roy

rules.case_name: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.reference: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Establishes the principle that the right to criticize judicial action is part of the freedom of speech and expression, provided it is fair and not scandalous. rules.reference: Principle of Conditional Apology in Contempt Proceedings

rules.case_name: Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat

Deals with the punishment for contempt. rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972

rules.case_name: Firms Amar Nath Basheshar Dass vs Tek Chand
