rules.case_name: Vineet Kumar vs Mangal Sain Wadhera
rules.reference: Vineet Kumar vs Mangal Sain Wadhera
rules.relevance: Relied upon by the appellant tenant to argue that the tenant is entitled to protection under the Act once the ten-year exemption period elapses, even if the suit was filed earlier, suggesting that the right to protection accrues upon the expiry of the exemption.

rules.reference: Accrual of Right to Protection under Rent Control Legislation
rules.relevance: The central legal principle to be decided is whether the right to protection under rent control laws is a substantive right that accrues only when the statutory conditions (expiry of exemption) are met, or whether it is a procedural right determined at the inception of the litigation.
Relevant for determining the exact commencement of the ten-year exemption period under Section 39, which is crucial for calculating whether the period had expired by the time of the trial or appeal.

rules.reference: Effect of Change in Law or Status during Pendency of Suit

rules.case_name: Management of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry v. R. K. Mittal

The specific provisions under which the complaint for prosecution was filed against the Secretary of FICCI for non-compliance with registration requirements.

rules.reference: Principle of Statutory Interpretation regarding 'Trade or Business'
rules.relevance: The legal test for determining whether an entity engaged in activities of general utility or charitable nature, funded by subscriptions and not distributing profits, constitutes a 'trade or business' or 'commercial establishment'.

rules.reference: Distinction between official acts and criminal acts
rules.relevance: A key legal principle relevant to Section 197 CrPC is that sanction is only required for acts done in the discharge of official duty. Acts that are purely criminal and have no connection with the official duty, even if committed by a public servant, do not require sanction. rules.reference: Interpretation of 'purporting to be done' in Section 197 CrPC

rules.reference: Nature of Criminal Misappropriation by Public Servant
rules.relevance: The court must consider whether the misappropriation of funds entrusted to a public servant in their official capacity is inherently an act done in the discharge of duty (requiring sanction) or a betrayal of that duty (not requiring sanction). This distinction is crucial for applying Section 197.

rules.reference: Effect of mistake in granting sanction

rules.reference: Burden of proof regarding official duty

rules.reference: Standard of Proof in Circumstantial Cases

The High Court rejected the extrajudicial confession to Ujagar Singh. The legal principle regarding the necessity of corroboration for extrajudicial confessions and the standard of scrutiny applied to such evidence is relevant to the first issue.

rules.relevance: The Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint. The legal principles governing when a magistrate can take cognizance of a complaint under Section 630 and the threshold for issuing process are relevant.

rules.case_name: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India

rules.case_name: State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co.
rules.reference: State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co.
rules.relevance: This case deals with the interpretation of 'sale' and the passing of property in the context of sales tax exemptions, providing guidance on how to determine the point of sale in complex contractual arrangements like FOB.

Defines 'dealer' and 'registered dealer'. This definition is crucial for interpreting Section 10(b) to determine if the phrase 'person to whom he has sold the goods' is restricted to registered dealers or includes unregistered persons.

The general commercial and legal principle that in FOB contracts, risk and property often pass upon shipment, but the specific intent of the parties and retention of documents (like the bill of lading) can alter this. This principle underpins the factual dispute regarding when property passed.
The procedural basis for the High Court's jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition challenging the Sales Tax Officer's assessment. While procedural, it frames the scope of the High Court's review.

Defines the nature of the firm M/s. Daulatram Rameshwarlal. Relevant for establishing the legal capacity of the appellant to sue and be sued, and the nature of the business entity involved in the transactions.

This is the central statutory provision in dispute. The High Court applied this article to hold that the appellants' title to specific properties was open to challenge because the limitation period for challenging alienations by a manager had not expired. The appeal challenges this application.

rules.reference: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
rules.relevance: The suit was filed under this section, which governs suits for declaration of title to properties alleged to be religious or charitable endowments. The interpretation of this section determines the jurisdiction and the nature of the claim.

The lower appellate court held that the appellants acquired title by adverse possession. The Supreme Court must determine whether the possession was adverse to the temple or if the appellants were holding the property as trustees/managers, which would negate adverse possession.

rules.reference: Distinction between Personal Inam and Religious Endowment
rules.relevance: The core factual dispute is whether the original grant was a personal Inam (private property) or a religious endowment (temple property). This distinction determines whether the Limitation Act provisions regarding temple managers apply or if general property laws apply.

The facts state that individuals other than the transferor were performing worship and acting as de facto managers for over 25 years. The legal status of these de facto managers and whether their actions bind the temple or affect the limitation period is crucial.

While Article 134 B is the specific provision cited by the High Court, Article 142 (suits for possession of immovable property) is the general limitation provision. The court may need to distinguish between the two to determine if the suit is barred by general limitation or the specific provision for temple properties.

rules.reference: Alienation of Temple Property by Manager
rules.relevance: The issue involves whether a manager can alienate temple property as his own private property. The legal principles governing the validity of such alienations and the rights of the temple to recover them are central to the case.

rules.reference: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
rules.relevance: This section defines 'Hindu religious institution' and 'trustee'. The definition helps determine if the Pachai Kandai Udayavar Temple qualifies as an institution under the Act and if the respondents were validly appointed trustees.

rules.reference: Constructive Notice and Title by Prescription
rules.relevance: The appellants claimed title through subsequent alienations and prescriptive title. The court must assess if the long possession and alienations created a valid title independent of the original grant's nature.

rules.reference: Notice by Assistant Commissioner for Hindu Religious Endowments (1948)
rules.relevance: This administrative notice is a key piece of evidence stating there were no legally constituted trustees and identifying de facto trustees. It supports the argument that the temple was not properly managed by the transferor, affecting the limitation calculation.

The petitioner filed the petition under this article for a writ of habeas corpus. The court must determine if it has the jurisdiction to entertain the petition after the High Court discharged the rule under Article 226.

The petitioner contends that the statutory provisions are void under this article as they violate fundamental rights. This is the basis for challenging the validity of the Income Tax Act and the Bombay City Land Revenue Act.

The central issue is whether Section 46(2) of the Income Tax Act and Section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act violate the right to equality by permitting discriminatory treatment or disparity in detention periods.
The petitioner argues that the detention violates the right to life and personal liberty. The court must assess if the procedure established by law for arrest and detention is valid.
The petitioner claims the detention violates protections against arrest and detention. The court must examine if the statutory procedure complies with the safeguards provided under this article.
This section directs the recovery of tax as if it were an arrear of land revenue. The petitioner challenges its validity under Article 14 for creating discriminatory treatment across states.
The warrant for arrest was issued under this section. The petitioner challenges its validity under Article 14 due to disparity in detention periods compared to other parts of the State.

The petitioner previously approached the Bombay High Court under this article. The High Court's decision to discharge the rule is part of the procedural history and may impact the Supreme Court's discretion under Article 32.
The petition seeks a writ of habeas corpus. The court must apply the legal principles governing this writ to determine if the detention is illegal or unconstitutional.

The court must apply principles of constitutional interpretation to determine if the challenged sections are void ab initio or if the discrimination alleged is reasonable classification under Article 14.

This is the primary fundamental right invoked by the appellants, guaranteeing the right to practice any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. The core of the appeal is whether the Act imposes an 'unreasonable restriction' on this right.

This provision empowers the State to impose reasonable restrictions on the right under Article 19(1)(g) in the interest of the general public. The Madras High Court relied on this to uphold the Act, and the Supreme Court must determine if the restrictions fall within this exception.

The appellants specifically challenge the licensing provisions under this section, arguing that the requirement to obtain licenses and the associated fees constitute an unreasonable restriction on their trade.

This section regulates trade allowances. The appellants argue that the bye-law prohibiting 'mahimai' is ultra vires this section because 'mahimai' is not a trade allowance, or that the prohibition exceeds the legislative power granted by this section.

The overarching legislation challenged for its validity. The court must assess whether the Act's objective of regulating markets and protecting producers justifies the restrictions imposed on traders.

rules.reference: Rules framed under the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933
rules.relevance: The specific bye-law challenged by the appellants. The court must decide if this rule is validly made under the Act and if it constitutes an unreasonable restriction on trade.

rules.provision: Rule prohibiting unregistered persons from carrying on business
rules.reference: Rules framed under the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933
rules.relevance: The Madras High Court had already struck down this specific rule. While partially resolved, it remains relevant context for the scope of valid regulations under the Act.
This Government Order extended the Act to Ramanathapuram and Tirunelveli Districts. Its validity is part of the challenge regarding the applicability of the Act to the appellants' area of operation.

This Government Order directed the constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar. The appellants challenge this notification, arguing that establishing a new market where a private one exists is an unreasonable restriction.

The central legal test to be applied. The court must determine if the restrictions imposed by the Act and Rules are 'reasonable' in the interest of the general public, balancing the trader's rights against the state's regulatory power.

rules.reference: Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This section empowers the Rent Controller to fix fair rent. The central issue is whether the Controller had jurisdiction to fix rent for vacant land when the superstructure ownership was disputed, and whether the subsequent order by the Court of Small Causes under this Act is binding.

This section deals with Res Judicata. The core legal question is whether the final order of the Court of Small Causes regarding the ownership of the superstructure and the validity of the rent fixation operates as res judicata in the subsequent civil suit for recovery of arrears.

rules.case_name: Life Insurance Corporation of India v. M/s. India Automobiles
rules.reference: Life Insurance Corporation of India v. M/s. India Automobiles
rules.relevance: This is the specific case described in the facts. The Supreme Court's decision in this appeal directly addresses whether the Rent Controller/Court of Small Causes had jurisdiction to decide title issues and whether their findings are binding on the civil court.

rules.reference: Jurisdiction of Rent Controller vs. Civil Court
rules.relevance: The principle that a Rent Controller is a statutory tribunal with limited jurisdiction. If the Controller lacks jurisdiction to decide complex questions of title to superstructures, their order may not be binding, or conversely, if they did decide it and it became final, it may bar re-litigation.

rules.reference: Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
rules.relevance: This section provides for appeals from the Rent Controller to the Court of Small Causes. The facts state the Court of Small Causes reversed the Controller's decision, making its order the final determination under the Act for the purpose of the appeal.

The legal principle determining whether a finding of fact or law by a statutory tribunal (like the Court of Small Causes acting as an appellate authority under the Rent Act) constitutes res judicata in a subsequent civil suit, particularly when the tribunal's jurisdiction to decide that specific issue is challenged.

Defines the rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee. Relevant to determining the nature of the lease (whether it was for land only or land and building) and the ownership of improvements/superstructures built by the tenant.

rules.reference: General Precedents on Res Judicata and Rent Control
rules.relevance: Supreme Court precedents establishing that if a Rent Controller or appellate court under the Rent Act finally decides an issue of title or ownership necessary for fixing rent, that decision is binding on the parties in subsequent proceedings, provided the tribunal had the jurisdiction to decide it.

Deals with questions relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of decrees. While the primary issue is res judicata under Section 11, Section 47 is relevant if the argument is that the civil suit is essentially an execution of the Rent Act order, though the facts suggest a fresh suit for arrears.

The principle that matters which were directly and substantially in issue in the former proceeding and were actually heard and decided must be deemed to have been directly and substantially in issue in the subsequent proceeding.

The core issue revolves around the omission of Sections 28 and 29 of the 1949 Act by the 1953 Amendment. These sections originally governed the procedure for ejectment suits and the role of the Controller. Their omission is argued to have rendered civil courts unable to entertain or remit such suits, thereby affecting the applicability of the Act to pending suits.

This section specifies the grounds for eviction. The appeal questions whether a landlord, in a suit instituted before the Act, must now establish these specific statutory grounds for eviction, or if the suit proceeds on the basis of the notice to quit served prior to the Act's commencement.

The 1953 Act substituted a new definition of 'thika tenant'. The lower appellate court held the respondent was a thika tenant under this amended definition. The relevance lies in determining if this new definition applies retrospectively to a suit already instituted and decreed.

This Ordinance preceded the 1953 Act and also substituted the definition of 'thika tenant'. It is relevant to the timeline of legislative changes and the potential transitional impact on pending litigation between 1952 and 1953.

rules.reference: Principle of Retrospective Operation of Statutes
rules.relevance: A fundamental principle of statutory interpretation is that statutes are presumed to operate prospectively unless a contrary intention appears. This principle is central to deciding whether the 1953 Amendment applies to a suit instituted in 1948 and decreed in 1949.

The distinction between substantive rights (which are generally not affected retrospectively) and procedural laws (which may apply to pending cases) is crucial. The appeal questions if the requirement to prove grounds under Section 3 is a substantive bar or a procedural requirement applicable to pending suits.

Section 6 of the General Clauses Act deals with the effect of repeal and savings. It is relevant to determine whether the repeal of Sections 28 and 29 of the 1949 Act saved the pending suit or extinguished the cause of action.

The landlord argues that the omission of Sections 28 and 29 rendered civil courts unable to remit suits, implying a lack of jurisdiction. Section 9 of the CPC affirms the jurisdiction of civil courts to try all suits of a civil nature unless expressly or impliedly barred.

rules.case_name: Keshavji Ramji v. Shamji Kishanji
rules.relevance: While not explicitly cited in the brief, this is a landmark Supreme Court case from the same period (1954) dealing with the retrospective operation of tenancy laws and the distinction between substantive and procedural changes. It is highly likely to be relevant authority for the Supreme Court's decision.

This section contains the original definitions. Comparing the original definition with the amended definition is necessary to determine if the respondent's status as a 'thika tenant' was altered by the 1953 Act, which is a prerequisite for the Act's application.

Central to the appellants' claim that property of wholly government-owned companies is exempt from property tax. The court must determine if the 'property of the Union' exemption applies to government companies.

rules.provision: Article 246 and Seventh Schedule (Entry 54 List I and Entry 49/50 List II)
rules.relevance: Relevant to the issue of legislative competence. The court must decide if the State Legislature had the power to tax lands used for coal mines, given that 'Mines and Minerals' fall under Union jurisdiction (Entry 54, List I), while 'Land Revenue' or 'Taxes on Lands and Buildings' typically fall under State jurisdiction.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973
rules.relevance: This section confers upon the Special Area Development Authority the powers of taxation that a Municipal Corporation has. The validity of the tax demand hinges on whether this delegation of power was valid and applicable to the amended Municipal Acts.

rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 / Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961
rules.relevance: These sections created the specific liability for property tax effective from April 1, 1976. The court must interpret whether the Authority, via Section 69(d) of the 1973 Act, could enforce these specific amendments enacted after the Authority's creation.

rules.case_name: Bharat Aluminium Co. Ltd. v. Special Area Development Authority
rules.reference: Bharat Aluminium Co. Ltd. v. Special Area Development Authority
rules.relevance: This is the actual case being described. The Supreme Court's judgment in this matter establishes the precedent regarding the competence of the Authority to levy tax and the applicability of Article 285 to government companies.

rules.case_name: State of Bombay v. United Motors (India) Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Bombay v. United Motors (India) Ltd.
rules.relevance: A foundational precedent interpreting Article 285. It distinguishes between 'property of the Union' and property owned by statutory corporations or government companies, often holding that government companies are separate legal entities and not automatically exempt under Article 285.

rules.provision: Section 617A (or relevant definition of Government Company)
rules.relevance: Defines the appellants as 'Government Companies'. This statutory definition is crucial to determine their legal status as separate juristic persons distinct from the Government of India, affecting the application of Article 285.

Relevant to resolving the conflict between State and Union legislative competence. The court may use this doctrine to determine if the true nature of the tax is on 'land' (State subject) or 'mines/minerals' (Union subject).

rules.reference: Privity of Contract and Estoppel against Statutory Authority
rules.relevance: Relevant to the appellants' argument based on the 1976 agreement. The court must decide if a statutory authority can be estopped from exercising its statutory taxing powers due to a private agreement, or if the agreement was ultra vires.

rules.case_name: Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India
rules.reference: Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Often cited in cases involving government companies to establish that they are distinct legal entities from the State, thereby limiting the direct application of constitutional immunities granted to the State itself.

Defines 'sales in the course of export' as sales that occasion the export or involve transfer of title after crossing customs frontiers. This is the primary benchmark to determine if the appellants' sales qualify for exemption from state purchase tax.

Deems the last sale preceding the export occasioning sale as a sale in the course of export if it complies with an export order. The core dispute is whether the appellants' sales are 'penultimate' sales under this section rather than direct export sales under Section 5(1).

The specific charging section for purchase tax on raw materials used in manufacturing. It provides an exemption if the manufactured goods are despatched outside the State by way of sale in the course of inter-State trade or export within the meaning of Section 5(1) of the CST Act. The applicability of this exemption is the central issue.

The general charging section for sales tax. The State argues that even if Section 9(1) does not apply, the purchases are taxable under this section. The relevance lies in determining if the general levy applies when specific exemptions fail.

Provides exemption from sales tax for certain purchases. The appellants relied on this section for their initial purchase of raw materials. Its interaction with the purchase tax liability under Section 9(1) is relevant to the second issue.

Defines 'turnover'. This definition is crucial for determining the scope of taxable transactions under the general charging Section 6 and whether the appellants' transactions fall within the taxable net.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. Shree Ram Agencies
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. Shree Ram Agencies
rules.relevance: A leading Supreme Court precedent interpreting Section 9(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act and its relationship with Section 5(1) and 5(3) of the CST Act. It establishes the distinction between sales occasioning export and penultimate sales, directly addressing the legal issue in this appeal.

rules.case_name: State of Haryana v. M/s. Shree Ram Agencies
rules.reference: State of Haryana v. M/s. Shree Ram Agencies (or similar precedents on Section 5(3))
rules.relevance: Precedents interpreting Section 5(3) of the CST Act are relevant to determine if the sale to the intermediate dealer constitutes a 'sale in the course of export' by deeming fiction, thereby potentially exempting the upstream purchase tax.

Relevant for interpreting the relationship between the State Act (Haryana Sales Tax Act) and the Central Act (CST Act). The court must harmonize the provisions to determine if the exemption in Section 9(1) extends to penultimate sales deemed as export sales under Section 5(3) of the CST Act.

rules.reference: Principle of Specific vs. General Levy
rules.relevance: Relevant to the second issue: whether the specific purchase tax provision (Section 9(1)) excludes the application of the general sales tax provision (Section 6). If the specific provision is inapplicable, the general provision may apply unless explicitly excluded.

Defines the formal requirements for the execution of a will, including the necessity of the testator signing or acknowledging the signature in the presence of two or more witnesses. This is the foundational statutory provision for determining if the will was validly executed.

Establishes that a testator must be of sound mind and not under coercion, undue influence, or fraud. The High Court's finding that the appellant failed to prove Lakshmamma's sound and disposing state of mind directly implicates this section.

rules.reference: Burden of Proof in Will Cases
rules.relevance: The legal principle that the propounder of a will bears the burden of proving its due execution and the testator's testamentary capacity. This is central to the issue of whether the appellant satisfied the burden despite suspicious circumstances.

The principle that when a will is surrounded by suspicious circumstances (such as the propounder drafting the will, unnatural dispositions, or artificial recitals), the burden on the propounder to prove due execution becomes heavier and must be discharged with greater care and precision.

The principle that if the person who benefits under the will (or their close relatives) is actively involved in its preparation, drafting, or attestation, it raises a presumption of undue influence or lack of free agency, requiring strict proof of the testator's independent volition.

The principle that dispositions which are unnatural or exclude natural heirs (such as grandchildren) in favor of strangers or distant relatives (such as the appellant's sons) are viewed with suspicion and require strong evidence to validate the testator's intent.

Defines the general rule of burden of proof, placing it on the person who asserts the existence of any fact. In this context, it supports the requirement for the appellant to prove the validity of the will.

Mandates the registration of wills affecting immovable property. While registration is not conclusive proof of validity, the fact that the will was registered on the same day is a relevant procedural fact in assessing the regularity of the transaction.

The principle that 'sound mind' for testamentary purposes means the ability to understand the nature of the act and its effects, and to form a rational judgment regarding the disposal of property. The High Court's doubt about Lakshmamma's mental state relies on this standard.

The principle that elaborate, artificial, or legally complex recitals in a will, especially when dictated by the propounder and not reflecting the testator's natural language or understanding, may indicate that the will does not represent the testator's true intentions.

This article empowers the appropriate authority to make rules for the recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union or a State. It is the foundational authority under which the Indian Ordnance Factories (Recruitment and Conditions of Service of Class III Personnel) Rules, 1956 were framed, governing the petitioners' service conditions.

rules.reference: Indian Ordnance Factories (Recruitment and Conditions of Service of Class III Personnel) Rules, 1956
rules.relevance: Rule 8 mandates that promotions be made based on a selection list prepared by Departmental Promotion Committees. This rule is central to determining whether the petitioners were entitled to automatic promotion under the superseded 1962 circular or if they were required to undergo the normal selection process as per the subsequent 1965/1966 orders.

rules.reference: Indian Ordnance Factories (Recruitment and Conditions of Service of Class III Personnel) Rules, 1956
rules.relevance: Rule 12 prohibits appointments otherwise than as specified in the Rules. This provision supports the argument that the executive circular of 1962 could not override the statutory rules regarding the mode of promotion, especially after it was superseded by subsequent government orders.

rules.case_name: Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981
rules.relevance: This is the specific precedent relied upon by the petitioners. The Supreme Court in this appeal directed promotion to Chargeman Grade II upon completion of two years of service based on the 1962 circular. The current appeal hinges on whether this relief extends to the present petitioners whose cases were governed by subsequent superseding orders.

rules.reference: Principle of 'No Pay for No Work'
rules.relevance: This legal principle, referenced in the Madhya Pradesh High Court judgment approved by the Supreme Court, dictates that employees granted backdated promotion are entitled to notional seniority and salary refixation but not to back wages. This is directly relevant to the second issue regarding the specific relief and back wages for the appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981.

rules.reference: Government Order dated 28th December 1965 and Circular dated 20th January 1966
rules.relevance: These executive instruments superseded the 1962 circular, stating that future promotions would be effected in accordance with normal rules. Their existence and timing are critical to determining whether the petitioners were eligible for the automatic promotion relief granted in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981.

rules.case_name: Madhya Pradesh High Court Judgment
rules.reference: Madhya Pradesh High Court Judgment (approved by Supreme Court)
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court approved this High Court judgment which held that backdated promotion entitles employees to notional seniority and salary refixation but not back wages. This precedent is directly applicable to deciding the consequential benefits and back wage claims in the current appeal.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Supersession of Executive Circulars
rules.relevance: This principle addresses the legal effect of a subsequent government order or circular that explicitly supersedes an earlier one. It is relevant to determining whether the rights accrued under the 1962 circular were extinguished for the petitioners by the 1965/1966 orders before their cases were considered.

rules.reference: Limitation and Laches in Writ Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The petitioners filed writ petitions in 1983, approximately 17 years after the relevant period of service. The principle of laches and limitation is relevant to assessing whether the delay in approaching the court bars the grant of relief, especially since the petitioners had already been promoted in the normal course in the interim.

This principle distinguishes between the benefits of notional seniority (which affects future promotions and seniority lists) and actual promotion (which involves holding the post and drawing pay). It is relevant to determining the extent of consequential benefits available to the appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981.

rules.reference: Goa, Daman & Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964
rules.relevance: The High Court held that this provision, introduced by the Fifth Amendment, ousted the jurisdiction of Civil Courts in favor of the Mamlatdar for disputes regarding agricultural land. The central issue is whether this ouster applies to suits pending at the time of the amendment.

The defendants contended that the second suit for restoration of possession was barred because the plaintiff had not claimed the same relief in the first suit (for declaration and injunction). The High Court agreed, making this rule central to the res judicata analysis.

The defendants raised the plea of res judicata, arguing that the matter of possession and title had been effectively decided or should have been decided in the first suit. The High Court ruled the suit was barred by res judicata.

rules.case_name: Keshavji Ramji v. Haribhai Desai
rules.relevance: A leading precedent on the interpretation of Order 2 Rule 2 CPC. It establishes that a plaintiff is not required to claim all reliefs arising from the same cause of action in one suit if the reliefs are distinct or if the cause of action for the second suit arises subsequently or is distinct in nature (e.g., declaration vs. possession).

rules.reference: Principle of Retrospective Operation of Statutes
rules.relevance: The core legal question is whether the Fifth Amendment to the Tenancy Act, which ousted civil court jurisdiction, applies retrospectively to suits already pending. General principles of statutory interpretation presume prospective operation unless expressly stated otherwise, especially regarding substantive rights and jurisdiction.

rules.reference: Goa, Daman & Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964
rules.relevance: To determine the jurisdiction of the Civil Court at the time the suit was instituted (1974), the state of the law before the 1976 amendment is relevant. If the Civil Court had jurisdiction when the suit was filed, the question is whether the subsequent amendment can strip that jurisdiction.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagwan Das
rules.relevance: This case deals with the distinction between a suit for declaration and a suit for possession. It supports the argument that a dismissal of a suit for declaration on technical grounds (like lack of possession) does not necessarily bar a subsequent suit for possession if the cause of action or the relief sought is distinct.

Although the primary issue is jurisdiction and res judicata, the procedural history involves the death of the plaintiff pendente lite. Order 21 Rule 103 governs the procedure for bringing on record legal representatives, which is relevant to the maintainability of the appeal by the appellants.

rules.reference: Distinction between Cause of Action for Declaration and Possession
rules.relevance: Legal principle that a suit for declaration of title and a suit for recovery of possession may constitute different causes of action, especially if the dispossession occurred after the institution of the first suit or if the first suit was dismissed on a technical ground unrelated to the merits of the possession claim.

rules.case_name: Rameshwar Prasad v. Ram Chandra
rules.relevance: Relevant for the proposition that when a special statute ousts the jurisdiction of civil courts, the civil court must dismiss the suit if the plea of tenancy is raised and substantiated, but this must be balanced against the principle that such ouster should not apply retrospectively to pending suits unless explicitly intended.
Central to the challenge that the reduction of retirement age is arbitrary, irrational, and unreasonable, violating the right to equality.
Relevant to the claim that the order violates equality of opportunity in matters of public employment by arbitrarily terminating services.
Defines the legislative power of the State to regulate the conditions of service of persons serving the Union or a State, which is the basis for the Government's authority to amend Fundamental Rules.
Crucial for determining whether the reduction of superannuation age amounts to 'removal' from service, thereby triggering the requirement of a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
Invoked by petitioners to argue that the termination of service violates the right to property (vested rights in service) without authority of law.
Challenged on the grounds that the arbitrary reduction of retirement age affects the livelihood and life of the employees.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Regulation of Conditions of Service) Ordinance, 1983
rules.relevance: The specific legislative instrument challenged for retrospectively validating the age reduction and deleting the protective proviso to Rule 2 of the Fundamental Rules.
The specific rule whose proviso was retrospectively deleted by the Ordinance; this proviso previously protected employees from modifications to conditions of service to their disadvantage.
The procedural basis under which the writ petitions were filed in the Supreme Court challenging the constitutional validity of the G.O. and Ordinance.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Vested Rights in Service
rules.relevance: A key legal principle to be examined to determine if employees who had already attained the age of 55 had a vested right to continue service until 58, which cannot be taken away by retrospective legislation.

This is the primary statutory provision under which the Company Law Board ordered the investigation. The appeal centers on the interpretation of this section, specifically whether the power can be exercised by the Chairman individually or requires the joint action of the Board, and the standard of 'reasonable cause' or 'circumstances suggesting' fraud required to invoke it.

The appellants challenged the order as violative of Article 14, alleging arbitrariness and mala fides. The court must determine if the exercise of power under Section 237(b) was arbitrary or discriminatory, thereby violating the guarantee of equality before law.

The appellants claimed the investigation order violated their right to practice any profession, trade, or business. The court must assess if the statutory power to investigate constitutes an unreasonable restriction on this fundamental right.

This article empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. The procedural history involves a writ petition filed under this article, and the scope of judicial review under Article 226 regarding administrative orders is relevant.

The appellants challenged the validity of the Chairman acting individually, alleging invalid sub-delegation. The court must apply legal principles regarding whether a statutory body's power can be delegated to a single member or if it must be exercised collectively, unless the statute expressly permits otherwise.

The appellants alleged the order was passed mala fide at the instance of the Finance Minister. The court must evaluate the evidence to determine if the subjective satisfaction of the Board was influenced by extraneous considerations or bad faith, which would vitiate the order.

rules.reference: Relevance of Material for Subjective Satisfaction
rules.relevance: The court must determine if the Company Law Board based its opinion on relevant circumstances suggesting fraud or misconduct, or if it relied on extraneous or irrelevant material. Administrative actions based on irrelevant considerations are legally invalid.

The broader context of Section 237, which empowers the Central Government or the Company Law Board to appoint inspectors, is relevant to understand the scope of authority and the conditions precedent for such an appointment.

rules.case_name: Barium Chemicals Ltd. v. Company Law Board
rules.reference: Barium Chemicals Ltd. v. Company Law Board
rules.relevance: This is the actual case being decided. The Supreme Court's judgment in this matter established key precedents regarding the interpretation of Section 237(b), the validity of the Chairman's individual action, and the scope of judicial review in such administrative matters.

The case involves the extent to which courts can interfere with the subjective satisfaction of a statutory body. The principle that courts generally do not substitute their opinion for that of the authority unless the decision is perverse, mala fide, or based on irrelevant grounds is central to the appeal.

This is the substantive provision under which the appellant was charged with criminal misconduct for possessing assets disproportionate to known sources of income. The core legal question is whether this section applies to High Court Judges.

This provision mandates previous sanction for prosecution of public servants. The central issue is identifying the 'authority competent to remove' a High Court Judge to grant such sanction, given the constitutional safeguards for judicial independence.

These articles define the removal process for Supreme Court and High Court Judges respectively. They are critical to determining who constitutes the 'authority competent to remove' a judge for the purpose of Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

This section defines 'public servant'. The appellant argues that Judges are not 'public servants' within the meaning of this definition because they do not fall under the master-servant relationship envisaged by the Act.

Although the charge was under 5(1)(e), Section 5(1)(d) (criminal misconduct) is often read in conjunction with 5(1)(e) to understand the scope of 'criminal misconduct' and the requirement of previous sanction under Section 6.

This is the procedural provision under which the appellant filed the application to quash the proceedings in the High Court. The validity of the High Court's dismissal of this application is part of the procedural history.

The appellant relies on the principle that Judges are constitutional functionaries and not subject to the same disciplinary or criminal liability mechanisms as ordinary public servants, particularly regarding the requirement of sanction from an authority that does not exist in the traditional sense for judges.

This section generally requires previous sanction for prosecution. The issue arises whether this requirement applies when the accused has ceased to be a public servant (retired) before the court takes cognizance of the offence.

rules.reference: Procedural Compliance in Disproportionate Assets Cases
rules.relevance: The appellant argues the charge sheet is invalid because the Investigating Officer did not formally call upon him to account for assets and record a finding on the satisfaction of his explanation. This touches upon the procedural requirements for establishing 'disproportionate assets' under the Act.

While the appeal is to the Supreme Court, the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 226 (or its inherent powers under CrPC) was exercised to dismiss the quashing petition. The scope of judicial review in criminal matters is a background principle.
